newsitem.title: USA: Dollar turns lower after U.S. open, focus on data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar turns lower after U.S. open, focus on data.

text.p: The dollar opened nearly flat but turned lower after a flurry of weaker-than-expected U.S. economic data dimmed hopes for another Federal Reserve interest rate hike in the near term, currency experts said.

U.S. durable goods orders unexpectedly fell 3.0 percent in March, the largest drop since August 1996. Furthermore, the 0.6 percent rise in the U.S. employment cost index in the first quarter was below the 0.9 percent gain expected, on average, in a Reuters poll.
"The reaction that the dollar's had is appropriate," said Elliott Dix, an assistant vice president at Signet Bank.

Dix noted a fear that "the markets (had) priced in another interest rate hike and this (data) may either delay that from happening, or in the worse case, this type of data will snow ball and the Fed will not have to raise rates."
Still, Dix said the softer-than-expected data are not a "dire" development for the U.S. dollar rally.
He doubted the data on its own is enough to eliminate the need for a rate hike in the "Fed's eyes".
The Fed already hiked its federal funds target rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25.
The dollar opened unchanged at 1.7320/30 marks. It stood at 126.80/85 yen, barely changed from 126.83/88 yen at Monday's close.
Shortly after the economic figures hit the market, the dollar slid near 1.7255 marks and 126.57 yen.
A trader at the New York branch of a Japanese bank attributed dollar/yen's slide to selling by interbank dealers.

At the same time, the trader noted that a large Japanese investor has interest to buy dollars much lower than the current level. The trader identified 125 yen as a level that might prompt the investor to purchase dollars.
Although the dollar's sold off after the softer-than-expected figures, some market participants held out hope that the currency could finish above where it is currently trading.
"I think you will see the dollar close higher than its current levels," said John Hazelton, chief dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank.
"It certainly won't move with the speed ... that the bond and the stock markets are moving, but the dollar should firm up and close higher on the day," he added.
Hazelton noted that there is general interest to buy dollars at lower levels, although the interest is not particularly aggressive.
Following the surprising economic reports, the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond rallied more than one point, while the Dow industrials surged more than 90 points.
In other trade, the dollar opened at 1.4740/50 Swiss francs, up from 1.4730/40 francs at the previous close.
Sterling slid to $1.6218/28 from $1.6242/52. The dollar opened at Canadian $1.4006/11, up from C$1.4001/06. The Australian dollar fell to $0.7795/00 from $0.7800/05.
